title: Trump Golf Trips Top 115 Million in Taxpayer Costs on Track for 300 Million by End of Term
synopsis: By August 2026, independent tracker estimates put Trumps second-term golf-related travel and security costs at nearly 115 million dollars, including 80 million for 59 days at Mar-a-Lago and 13.6 million for Bedminster. Trump visited his own properties on 191 of his first 512 days in office, or 37 percent of the time. At his pace the tracker projects 300 million total by end of term, doubling his first-term total.

title: Kushner Solicits 5 Billion From Saudi Arabia While Serving as Unpaid Mideast Envoy
synopsis: In early 2026, Jared Kushner firm Affinity Partners, already backed by 2 billion dollars from Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund, began soliciting 5 billion or more in new Saudi funds while Kushner simultaneously served as Trumps de facto Middle East envoy negotiating Gaza and Ukraine cease-fires. As a volunteer, Kushner is exempt from federal financial disclosure laws. Affinity 6.1 billion in assets are 99 percent from non-U.S. investors, primarily Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Qatar.

title: Trump 2025 Financial Disclosure Shows 2 Billion Income Including 1.2 Billion From Crypto
synopsis: Trumps June 2026 financial disclosure showed more than 2 billion dollars in income in 2025, triple the prior year, with 1.2 billion from crypto ventures including World Liberty Financial and meme coins. The UAE government bought a 500 million dollar stake in World Liberty, and separately invested 2 billion in Trumps stablecoin. A UAE property generated 10.4 million in fees. Ethics watchdogs noted Trump explicitly rejected the conflict-of-interest protections his predecessors had adopted.

title: CREW Reports Trump Earns Record 117 Million in Foreign Revenue in 2025
synopsis: CREW July 2026 analysis of Trumps financial disclosure found he earned over 117 million dollars from foreign business interests in 2025, nearly matching his entire first-term total in a single year. UAE revenue alone exceeded 32 million. Trump struck eight foreign property deals in his second term first year including deals in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Vietnam, Romania, and India, many with companies tied to foreign governments whose policies Trump was simultaneously shaping.

title: Qatar Gifts Trump 400 Million Luxury Jet Raising Foreign Emoluments Clause Concerns
synopsis: In May 2025, reports emerged that Qatar was gifting Trump a 400 million dollar Boeing 747 luxury aircraft for use as Air Force One. Legal experts immediately flagged violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause, which requires congressional approval for gifts from foreign governments to U.S. officials. The deal coincided with major U.S.-Qatar diplomatic activity and Qatar 2 billion dollar investment in the Trump stablecoin.

sources.title: Qatar gifting Trump $400M luxury jet raises ethical and legal concerns | PBS News

title: Trump Calls SCOTUS Justices 'Fools, Lapdogs, Disloyal' Over Tariff Ruling
synopsis: On February 20, 2026, after the Supreme Court voted 6-3 to strike down his sweeping global tariffs, Trump launched an extraordinary White House tirade calling six justices a 'disgrace to our nation' and 'very unpatriotic and disloyal to the Constitution.' He personally attacked two justices he had nominated — Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett — saying their decision was 'an embarrassment to their families,' and baselessly alleged the majority was 'swayed by foreign interests.' Chief Justice Roberts later said the attacks 'have got to stop.'

sources.title: Trump lashes out at his own Supreme Court picks over tariff ruling: "An embarrassment to their families" - CBS News

title: Senate Holds 'Rogue Judges' Impeachment Hearing Targeting Boasberg and Boardman
synopsis: On January 7, 2026, the Senate Judiciary subcommittee chaired by Ted Cruz held a hearing titled 'Impeachment: Holding Rogue Judges Accountable,' pushing to remove U.S. District Judges James Boasberg and Deborah Boardman for rulings against the Trump administration. Cruz sent a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson demanding the House advance impeachment proceedings. Georgetown law professor Stephen Vladeck testified that in U.S. history no judge had ever been impeached purely for the substance of their rulings, calling the move constitutionally unprecedented.

title: 97% of Trump Emergency SCOTUS Filings Claim Presidential Power Over Judiciary
synopsis: A Reuters analysis published March 7, 2026, found that 97% of the Trump administration's emergency Supreme Court filings argued that federal judges were intruding on presidential powers — compared to only 26% of comparable Biden-era filings. The administration raced to the Supreme Court with dozens of emergency requests to override lower-court judges who had blocked policies as unlawful. Legal experts described it as a systematic campaign to structurally diminish judicial independence.

sources.title: How Donald Trump is pushing the Supreme Court to weaken federal judges | Reuters

title: DAG Todd Blanche Declares 'It's a War' Against Federal Judges
synopsis: Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche publicly stated at a Federalist Society event that confrontation with the judiciary is 'a war, man,' claiming a group of 'repeat player' judges was 'intentionally' blocking Trump's agenda. Blanche said judges were 'just not following the law, full stop.' The remarks contributed to the record surge in death threats against federal judges — 400 targeted in 2025 alone, a 78% increase over four years.

title: Trump Threatens to 'Pack the Court' After Losing Tariff and Birthright Cases
synopsis: On May 14, 2026, Trump posted on Truth Social threatening to pack the Supreme Court after multiple rulings against him, writing 'I should be the one wanting to PACK THE COURT!' He accused justices he appointed — Gorsuch and Barrett — of showing 'so little respect' and claimed he 'put certain people on the Supreme Court who totally misrepresented who they were.' Legal analysts noted Congress could expand the Court through ordinary legislation, making the threat credible.

title: Trump Admin Violated Court Orders in at Least 31 Lawsuits in 15 Months
synopsis: An Associated Press investigation published May 2, 2026, documented that in the first 15 months of Trump's second term, district court judges found the administration in violation of court orders in at least 31 separate lawsuits — covering mass layoffs, deportations, immigration practices, and spending cuts. In one case, Judge Sunshine Sykes accused Trump officials of seeking to 'erode any semblance of separation of powers,' saying the conduct was only possible 'in a world where the Constitution does not exist.'

sources.title: Trump officials show extraordinary defiance of court rulings | AP News

title: 'Big Beautiful Bill' Strips Courts of Power to Enforce Contempt Against Government
synopsis: Trump's sweeping tax-and-spending 'Big Beautiful Bill,' passed in May 2025, contained a provision preventing any federal court — including the Supreme Court — from enforcing contempt orders against the government unless plaintiffs first post a monetary bond. Critics said the one-sentence provision, embedded in the 1,100-page bill, retroactively rendered judges powerless to punish the administration for defying court orders, representing a legislative gutting of judicial enforcement authority.

sources.title: Republican attempt to rein in federal judges is stripped from Trump's big bill

title: 77 Federal Judges Across Party Lines Have Criticized Trump for Acting Unlawfully
synopsis: A CNN analysis published June 22, 2026, identified at least 77 court rulings in which federal judges — including many appointed by Republican presidents and by Trump himself — accused the administration of acting unlawfully, disregarding constitutional limits, retaliating against political opponents, or openly defying court orders. The rulings came from 69 different judges and clustered around three patterns: abuse of power, bad faith conduct, and contempt of court.

title: Death Threats Against Federal Judges Surge 78% — 400 Targeted in One Year
synopsis: Reporting by CBS News (March 2, 2026) and the ABA Journal (July 27, 2026) confirmed that 400 federal judges were targets of serious threats in 2025, a 78% jump from four years earlier. Judge John Coughenour received dozens of death threats after blocking Trump's birthright citizenship order; he was also swatted and received a bomb threat. Judge Esther Salas said pizzas were delivered to her home addressed to her murdered son's name as a doxxing threat.

sources.title: More federal judges warn of an increase in violent threats

title: Trump Demands Loyalty From Justices, Blasts Own Nominees as 'Misrepresenting' Ideology
synopsis: After the Supreme Court's February 2026 tariff ruling, Trump stated he put justices on the court 'who totally misrepresented who they were' and demanded they show loyalty. His State of the Union address featured three majority justices sitting expressionless while Trump condemned the ruling as 'very unfortunate.' The explicit expectation of judicial fealty was widely described by constitutional scholars as an authoritarian corruption of judicial independence.

sources.title: Trump lashes out at his own Supreme Court picks over tariff ruling: "An embarrassment to their families" - CBS News

title: Rep. Ogles Files Impeachment Resolution Against Judge Burroughs Over Somali TPS Ruling
synopsis: On August 3, 2026, Rep. Andy Ogles (R-TN) filed an impeachment resolution against U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs after she issued a stay blocking the Trump administration from ending Temporary Protected Status for Somali nationals. DHS General Counsel James Percival also attacked the ruling publicly, calling it 'defiance, obstruction, and delay.' The resolution was the latest in a pattern of Trump allies filing judicial impeachment threats after unfavorable rulings.

title: DOJ Sues 27 Sanctuary Jurisdictions — Largest State-Federal Coercion Campaign in U.S. History
synopsis: By July 17, 2026, the Trump Justice Department had filed 27 lawsuits against more than 20 cities, counties, and states with sanctuary policies limiting local police cooperation with ICE — targeting Connecticut, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Michigan, and Philadelphia. Federal judges had dismissed at least four of these suits as unconstitutional overreach. The campaign used the Supremacy Clause as the legal basis for forcing state law enforcement to participate in federal deportation operations.

title: 24 States Sue Trump Over Conditions Tying Disaster Relief to Election and Immigration Compliance
synopsis: On July 23, 2026, a coalition of 24 state attorneys general plus the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration for conditioning billions in FEMA and DHS disaster preparedness grants on states adopting Trump's preferred election systems and immigration enforcement policies. California alone receives $150 million annually in HSGP funding; the conditions required states to verify voter citizenship through a federal system or lose 20% of grants.

title: Trump Calls for Terminating Senate Filibuster to Ram Through Pro-GOP Agenda
synopsis: In April 2026 Trump posted a lengthy Truth Social rant demanding Senate Republicans 'terminate the filibuster' — the 60-vote threshold required to advance most legislation — warning that Democrats were 'Country Destroying Sleazebags' who would dominate for '100 years' if reform wasn't passed. Scholars noted the filibuster had long been the last structural check on one-party rule in the Senate.

sources.title: Under pressure from Trump, can the filibuster survive 2026? : NPR

title: AG Pam Bondi Files Misconduct Complaint Against Judge Boasberg; Admin Uses Shadow Docket 34 Times
synopsis: Attorney General Pam Bondi filed a formal judicial misconduct complaint against Chief Judge James Boasberg after he held the administration in contempt for defying its order halting deportations under the Alien Enemies Act. A Brennan Center analysis found that as of March 2026 the Trump administration had invoked the Supreme Court's emergency shadow docket 34 times in 14 months — more than the Biden, Obama, and George W. Bush administrations combined — winning 80% of those emergency requests.

title: DOGE Storms 15+ Federal Agencies in First 100 Days
synopsis: Beginning January 20, 2025, DOGE operatives — many recruited from Musk's private companies — fanned out into over 15 federal agencies, demanding full access to sensitive systems without congressional authorization. They fired more than 100,000 government employees including scientists, public health experts, and diplomats. Reuters documented 20 instances where cuts created purchasing bottlenecks, paralysis, and brain drains rather than savings.

title: DOGE Accessed Treasury Payment Systems Without Security Controls
synopsis: A GAO report (GAO-26-108131) found that DOGE employees were granted broad access to Bureau of Fiscal Service payment systems — which process trillions in federal payments — without proper cybersecurity controls. On January 30, 2025, a DOGE employee emailed unencrypted USAID payment data containing PII to GSA DOGE members without authorization. BFS failed to implement 9 of 14 critical security controls required to protect sensitive information.

sources.title: Treasury watchdog begins audit of DOGE team's access to US government's payment system | AP News

title: DOGE Shared SSA Data to Unauthorized Server, Violated Court Order
synopsis: Court filings in January 2026 revealed DOGE employees at the Social Security Administration secretly shared sensitive data on millions of Americans via unauthorized third-party servers, violating both agency policy and a federal court's March 2025 restraining order. The SSA admitted it cannot determine what data was exfiltrated or whether it still exists on external servers. A whistleblower alleged DOGE copied a dataset of 300 million Americans' sensitive information into a private cloud without security protocols.

sources.title: Whistleblower says DOGE put Social Security numbers at risk : NPR

title: DOGE SSA Employees Tried to Share Data With Voter Fraud Group
synopsis: Court filings from January 2026 revealed that two DOGE employees at the Social Security Administration were approached by a political advocacy group seeking to cross-reference Social Security data with state voter rolls to find evidence of voter fraud. One DOGE staffer signed a Voter Data Agreement and sent it to the group without SSA knowledge on March 24, 2025 — the same day officials told a court all DOGE data access had been terminated.

sources.title: How DOGE improperly accessed and shared Social Security data : NPR

title: SSA Inspector General Probes DOGE Employee Retaining 'God-Level' Data
synopsis: In March 2026, the Social Security Administration's Inspector General launched a formal investigation after a whistleblower alleged a former DOGE software engineer retained copies of two tightly restricted national databases — including the NUMIDENT containing records on nearly every American — on a thumb drive, and claimed 'God-level' access to SSA systems. The former employee allegedly planned to share the data with their new private-sector employer.

sources.title: New investigations look at DOGE and Social Security data : NPR

title: Musk's DOGE Pushed His Own Grok AI Into Federal Agencies
synopsis: Reuters reported on May 23, 2025 that DOGE operatives were expanding the use of Musk's own Grok AI chatbot across federal agencies — including DHS — without approval, to analyze sensitive government data. Five technology and privacy specialists warned the arrangement potentially violated conflict-of-interest laws, security statutes, and put sensitive information about millions of Americans at risk. No conflict-of-interest waiver for Musk was ever made public.

sources.title: Exclusive: Musk’s DOGE expanding his Grok AI in US government, raising conflict concerns | Reuters

title: Starlink Given Inside Track on $2.4B FAA Contract Held by Verizon
synopsis: AP reported on February 25, 2025 that Musk's Starlink was installed in FAA facilities as a prelude to displacing Verizon's competitively awarded $2.4 billion, 15-year air traffic communications contract. Musk had publicly attacked the Verizon contract on X while simultaneously serving as a senior White House adviser. Senators including Maria Cantwell warned that Musk appeared to be directing policy to benefit his own company in what they called 'serious red flags.'

sources.title: Musk slams a Starlink competitor amid questions about $2.4B FAA contract

title: SpaceX Positioned as Frontrunner for 'Golden Dome' Missile Defense
synopsis: A group of 42 Democratic lawmakers led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren requested a Defense Department Inspector General probe in May 2025 into Elon Musk's role in the bidding process for the 'Golden Dome' missile defense system. Reuters reported SpaceX, along with Palantir and Anduril, had emerged as frontrunners for the project while Musk was simultaneously serving as a senior White House adviser overseeing agencies that would oversee SpaceX contracts.

sources.title: Musk’s SpaceX is frontrunner to build Trump’s ‘Golden Dome’ missile shield

title: DOGE Targeted 875 VA Contracts Including Cancer Care and PTSD Programs
synopsis: In late February 2025, DOGE presented the VA with a list of 875 contracts to terminate. The full AP-obtained list showed cuts would eliminate cancer care monitoring, toxic exposure assessment, electronic health record upgrades, and the National Center for PTSD. After a revolt by VA employees, the list was reduced to 585, but employees said the remaining cancellations would still cause harm to veterans and VA care and benefits.

sources.title: DOGE plans to cut VA contracts may harm veterans' care, employees say

title: DOGE Closed Social Security Offices, Left Disabled Facing 135-Mile Trips
synopsis: By February 2025, DOGE began closing at least 10 Social Security field offices, including the White Plains, NY hearing office serving seven counties with 2,000 pending cases. Closure would force elderly and disabled beneficiaries to travel up to 135 miles to the next office, potentially into another state. SSA staffing was already at a 50-year low when DOGE arrived, and ProPublica reported many closures targeted low-income, disabled, and orphaned recipients with no internet access.

title: USAID Shutdown Blamed for 'Countless Deaths' Worldwide
synopsis: DOGE's effective elimination of the U.S. Agency for International Development — which provided humanitarian aid, disaster relief, and global health services — was described by multiple congressional reports as having caused countless deaths across the world. The agency was gutted in early 2025 without congressional approval. NPR's year-end review confirmed the agency was effectively eliminated by the end of 2025, along with the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and much of the Education Department.

title: DOGE Accessed Competitors' Trade Secrets via Federal Data Systems
synopsis: A Washington Post investigation published June 30, 2025 found that DOGE secured viewing access to sensitive records in at least seven major federal departments containing competitors' trade secrets, nonpublic government contract details, and sensitive regulatory information. Competitors in industries overlapping Musk's empire — including AI, space, and medical devices — were alarmed about potential exposure. The Post found no conflict-of-interest waiver was ever obtained by Musk for any of these access grants.

sources.title: DOGE has the keys to sensitive data that could help Elon Musk - Washington Post

title: DOGE Overstated $110B in Savings; Auditors Find Figures Fabricated
synopsis: An AP report from August 6, 2026 revealed that government auditors found DOGE systematically overstated savings on its public Wall of Receipts website. DOGE had reported $110 billion in savings but auditors found the figures included contracts already canceled before DOGE existed and amounts that were never obligated. Meanwhile, total federal outlays for fiscal year 2025 reached $7 trillion — higher than 2024's $6.7 trillion.

sources.title: Just how much has DOGE exaggerated its numbers? Now we have receipts.

title: Musk Departs DOGE After Criticizing Trump's Spending Bill
synopsis: Elon Musk's off-boarding from DOGE began the night of May 28, 2025, after he publicly criticized Trump's 'Big Beautiful Bill' spending package as undermining DOGE's work. Reuters reported Musk did not have a formal conversation with Trump before announcing his exit. At departure, DOGE's website claimed $175 billion in savings — a fraction of the trillions Musk had promised — and the national debt had grown by more than $2.2 trillion during the same fiscal year.

sources.title: Musk says Trump's tax bill undermines DOGE

title: DOGE Formally Shuts Down July 4, 2026; Musk Says 'I Got Carried Away'
synopsis: DOGE formally ended operations on July 4, 2026, over a year after Musk's own departure in May 2025. In a July 23, 2026 Economist interview, Musk admitted 'I think I got a little too involved in politics. Got carried away, frankly.' By that point, 317,000 federal workers had been pushed out of government, the national debt exceeded $38 trillion, and federal spending had actually increased year-over-year despite DOGE's stated mission.

title: 170+ US Citizens Detained by ICE in Mass Sweeps, Held Incommunicado
synopsis: A ProPublica investigation published in October 2025 documented over 170 cases in which US citizens were detained by immigration agents during the first nine months of Trump's second term. More than 50 were held after agents questioned their citizenship status — nearly all Latino — and more than 20 were held for over a day without being able to contact lawyers or family. Citizens were tackled, beaten, pepper-sprayed, tased, and shot. ICE Director Todd Lyons privately admitted arrests of citizens served as 'a deterrent,' while publicly ICE officials denied any citizens had been mistakenly detained.

sources.title: Democrats to Investigate Immigration Agents Detaining of American Citizens — ProPublica

title: Brian Morales Garcia, Born in Denver, Deported to Mexico as 'Illegal Alien'
synopsis: On April 3, 2026, Texas state troopers pulled over an HVAC worker near Fredericksburg for a window tint violation and called ICE. Brian José Morales Garcia, 25, born in Denver with a Colorado birth certificate and Social Security card, was detained, coerced into signing deportation papers after 5 days in 5 different facilities, and deported to Mexico on April 7. DHS claimed he 'admitted to entering illegally' — a statement his attorney said was coerced under duress. The Austin American-Statesman independently corroborated his birth certificate.

sources.title: ICE deported man to Mexico who says he’s a U.S. citizen

title: US Citizen Leo Garcia Venegas Detained by ICE Three Times in One Year
synopsis: Leonardo Garcia Venegas, a US citizen of Mexican descent in Alabama, was detained by immigration agents three separate times — in 2025 and again on May 2, 2026 — despite presenting a valid Alabama REAL ID each time. Agents dismissed the REAL ID as fake, tackled and shackled him. ICE officials at a border security conference the same week falsely stated citizens had been detained 'zero times' by mistake. Venegas filed a federal lawsuit; the government argued the sweeps were constitutionally valid.

sources.title: Why Have Immigration Agents Detained American Leo Garcia Venegas Three Times? — ProPublica

title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Wrongfully Deported to CECOT Torture Prison
synopsis: On March 12, 2025, Kilmar Abrego Garcia — a Maryland resident with a 2019 court order protecting him from deportation, whose wife and 5-year-old child are US citizens — was arrested by ICE and deported to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison on March 15 in what the administration acknowledged was an 'administrative error.' The administration refused to return him for months. Court filings allege he was subjected to severe beatings and torture at CECOT, losing 30 lbs in two weeks, forced to kneel from 9 PM to 6 AM with guards striking anyone who collapsed.

sources.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia suffered psychological and physical torture in El Salvador prison, attorneys say

title: 238 Venezuelans Mass-Deported to CECOT Using Tattoo 'Gang Points System'
synopsis: On March 15, 2025, the Trump administration invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to deport 238 Venezuelan men to El Salvador's CECOT prison with no individual due process hearings. ProPublica found nearly half — 118 men — were deported while active immigration cases were pending. The government used a secret 'points system' assigning gang membership based on tattoos including roses, crowns, and family names. Andry Hernández, a gay barber whose wrist tattoos of 'mom' and 'dad' with crowns earned 5 points, was photographed on his knees in chains crying as guards slapped him.

sources.title: Who Are the Venezuelan Immigrants Trump Sent to CECOT? — ProPublica

title: Supreme Court: Trump Gave Venezuelan Deportees Only 24-Hour Due Process Notice
synopsis: In A.A.R.P. v. Trump (May 16, 2025), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the Trump administration provided constitutionally inadequate notice before deporting Venezuelan detainees under the Alien Enemies Act. Evidence showed the government had transported detainees to an airport before a midnight court order halted removals. The court found notice 'devoid of information about how to exercise due process rights' was unconstitutional. The administration had argued in the Abrego Garcia case that it could not return someone already deported, signaling deportation was being used as a permanent evasion strategy.

sources.title: Supreme Court rules administration must give Venezuelans more time to challenge deportation under Alien Enemies Act

title: Trump Deports Immigrants to South Sudan and Libya — Countries They Are Not From
synopsis: Beginning in early 2025, the Trump administration began deporting immigrants to 'third countries' — nations they were not citizens of — without notifying them or allowing them to contest being sent to war zones. In May 2025, men from Myanmar, Laos, Vietnam, Cuba, and Mexico were placed on a flight to South Sudan with less than 16 hours' notice. Secretary of State Rubio admitted in a court filing that blocking the practice threatened 'a significant commercial deal to expand activities of a US energy company in Libya.' The Supreme Court allowed such deportations to continue on June 23, 2025.

sources.title: Third-country deportations ramp up to countries like South Sudan : NPR

title: Camp East Montana: Beatings, Extrajudicial Killing, Enforced Disappearances at Fort Bliss
synopsis: Camp East Montana, opened in August 2025 at Fort Bliss military base in El Paso, became the site of systematic abuse documented in a July 2026 Human Rights Watch/ACLU report. Of 71 detainees interviewed, 90% had been beaten or witnessed beatings by masked guards with no name tags. On January 3, 2026, Geraldo Lunas Campos, 55, a Cuban father of four, was handcuffed and asphyxiated to death by guards in solitary confinement after asking for medication. A local medical examiner ruled his death a homicide; a GAO report found evidence was 'missing or destroyed.'

title: 52 Deaths in ICE Custody in 500 Days — Mortality Rate at 20-Year High
synopsis: Between January 20, 2025 and June 4, 2026, 52 people died in ICE custody — a mortality rate more than double Trump's first term and nearly four times the Biden administration's rate, according to a Human Rights Watch report published June 25, 2026. At least 17 deaths were linked to medical staff delaying or withholding critical care; people died from undiagnosed lymphoma, untreated AIDS, alcohol withdrawal, and suicide after wellness check failures. The detention population grew 77% but deaths grew by over 138%. ICE oversight offices were gutted under the Trump administration.

sources.title: 2025 was ICE’s deadliest year in two decades. Here are the 32 people who died in custody | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian

title: Trump Fires 200 Immigration Judges, Replacing Them with Military Lawyers
synopsis: The Trump administration fired, forced out, or eliminated approximately 202 of the nation's 726 immigration judges between February 2025 and early 2026, reducing the judiciary by nearly a quarter. By February 2026, 12 immigration courts had lost over half their judges and two courts had zero permanent judges. To replace them, EOIR scrapped the requirement for immigration expertise and requested 600 military lawyers to serve as temporary judges. The national immigration case backlog reached nearly 4 million cases, with new hearings scheduled as far out as 2030.

sources.title: The Trump administration fired nearly 100 immigration judges in 2025. What's next? : NPR

title: Mahmoud Khalil: Green Card Holder Detained 104 Days for Leading Campus Protest
synopsis: On March 8, 2025, ICE agents arrested Mahmoud Khalil, 30, a Palestinian Columbia University graduate student and lawful permanent US resident, at his campus apartment. The Trump administration revoked his green card citing an obscure foreign policy statute, claiming his pro-Palestinian protest activities in 2024 created 'adverse foreign policy consequences.' Trump called the arrest 'the first of many to come.' Khalil's US citizen wife gave birth while he was held 1,300 miles away in Louisiana for 104 days. A federal judge ordered his release in June 2025.

sources.title: Mahmoud Khalil: Palestinian activist shares ‘dehumanizing’ experience of months in ICE detention | CNN

title: 100+ US Citizen Children Left Stranded as ICE Deports Parents Without Warning
synopsis: A CNN investigation published September 2025 identified more than 100 US citizen children — from newborns to teenagers — who were left stranded after ICE deported their parents, often with virtually no notice. In one case, a 4-year-old with Stage 4 cancer was deported to Honduras without medication or the ability to contact doctors. A New York Times investigation in August 2025 documented ICE using a deliberate tactic of separating children to coerce parents into 'voluntary' departure, with written notes stating 'Interior separation is approved.'

sources.title: ‘The new family separation crisis’: More than 100 US citizen kids left stranded by ICE enforcement actions, CNN finds | CNN Politics

title: Pregnant Women Shackled During Miscarriages in ICE Detention Centers
synopsis: Despite official ICE policy against detaining pregnant women for civil immigration violations, documentation by the ACLU and National Immigration Project published in October 2025 showed over a dozen pregnant women suffering medical neglect in immigration detention. One woman identified as Lucia experienced heavy vaginal bleeding for hours without medical attention, was taken shackled to an emergency room requiring a blood transfusion after a miscarriage, and was then returned to ICE custody. Congressional requirements to report statistics on detained pregnant women had been eliminated.

sources.title: Pregnant women describe miscarrying and bleeding out while in ICE custody, advocates say

title: DHS Requests 20,000 National Guard Troops for Domestic Interior Immigration Raids
synopsis: On May 9, 2025, the Department of Homeland Security formally requested 20,000–21,000 National Guard troops from the Pentagon to conduct 'expansive interior immigration enforcement operations' across the United States — the first such domestic request in US history. The 21-page request included tasks such as fugitive tracking with 'night operations and rural interdictions,' surveillance and canvassing missions, and transporting detainees between states. Defense officials warned the deployment could violate the Posse Comitatus Act if federalized.

sources.title: DHS asks for 20,000 National Guard troops for immigration roundups | AP News

title: Trump Ends 14-Year Protection Against ICE Arrests at Churches and Schools
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman rescinded the Obama-era policy barring ICE from making immigration arrests at 'sensitive locations' — schools, hospitals, churches, mosques, and synagogues — a protection in place since 2011. A federal judge in Maryland temporarily blocked the policy as applied to approximately 1,700 houses of worship in 35 states in February 2025, finding it was preventing people from attending religious services. School enrollment dropped in immigrant-heavy communities as families kept children home out of fear.

sources.title: Trump administration throws out policies limiting arrests of migrants at sensitive locations | AP News

title: Trump Bans AP from Press Pool Over 'Gulf of America' Refusal
synopsis: Beginning February 11, 2025, the White House barred Associated Press journalists from the presidential press pool — blocking access to the Oval Office, Mar-a-Lago events, and Air Force One — after the AP declined to adopt Trump's renamed 'Gulf of America' in its stylebook. Trump confirmed on February 18 that the ban would continue 'until such time as they agree.' The AP sued three Trump officials on February 21 citing First Amendment violations. A federal judge ruled in the AP's favor but the White House responded with a workaround policy rather than compliance.

sources.title: AP journalists barred from Air Force One over style dispute | AP News

title: White House Seizes Control of Presidential Press Pool Selection
synopsis: On February 25, 2025, press secretary Karoline Leavitt announced the Trump administration would itself determine which news organizations participate in the presidential press pool — ending a century of independent journalist control over pool membership. The move marked the first time in modern history that a U.S. administration unilaterally claimed authority over who could cover the president up close. The White House Correspondents' Association announced it would not distribute pool reports from administration-chosen correspondents, calling the move a threat to an independent press.

sources.title: White House takes control of the press pool covering Trump

title: FCC Reinstates Broadcast Complaints Against ABC, CBS, NBC on Day Two of Trump Term
synopsis: On January 22, 2025, just two days after inauguration, new FCC Chairman Brendan Carr reinstated complaints against ABC over its 2024 presidential debate moderation, CBS over a '60 Minutes' Kamala Harris interview, and NBC over a Harris appearance on SNL — all previously dismissed as unconstitutional weaponization of licensing authority. Critics warned the move was designed to intimidate broadcast networks. House Democrats opened a formal probe into the investigations by March 31, 2025, calling them 'sham' proceedings to suppress press freedom.

title: DOJ Reversal Allows Seizure of Journalists' Phone Records and Testimony
synopsis: On April 25, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued an internal memo rescinding Biden-era protections that had barred prosecutors from seizing reporters' phone records, emails, and compelling journalist testimony in leak investigations. The new policy explicitly allows subpoenas, court orders, and search warrants targeting news media. The memo indicated investigations could be launched not just for classified leaks but for disclosures that 'undermine' Trump administration policies — a far broader standard. Press freedom groups called it a landmark threat to investigative journalism and source protection.

sources.title: In reversal, US Justice Department says media records can be seized in leak probes

title: Wire Services AP, Reuters, Bloomberg Stripped of Permanent Press Pool Slot
synopsis: On April 15, 2025, the White House announced that AP, Reuters, and Bloomberg News — wire services that together reach billions of readers — would lose their permanent reserved spot in the daily presidential press pool. The move came one week after a federal judge ruled in the AP's favor in its lawsuit over access, and was widely seen as a workaround to evade the court order. The AP filed an emergency motion on April 16 arguing the new policy violated the ruling by still giving the administration sole discretion over access.

sources.title: In latest media crackdown, White House limits newswire access to Trump

title: Hegseth Orders Pentagon Reporters to Have Escorts, Bars Free Movement
synopsis: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued orders on May 23, 2025, requiring all credentialed journalists to have official government escorts to access most of the Pentagon building, ending decades of independent reporting from the world's largest office building. The Pentagon Press Association called the measures a 'direct attack on the freedom of the press.' The restrictions required prior approval for any reporter movement within DoD headquarters, though no specific security breach had prompted the change.

sources.title: Hegseth orders more restrictions on press at Pentagon | AP News

title: FBI Launches Probe Into 2022 Dobbs Leak to Intimidate Journalists

title: FCC Forces CBS to Install Government-Backed 'Bias Monitor' in Newsroom

title: Congress Defunds NPR and PBS, Cutting $1.1 Billion in Public Broadcasting

title: 30+ News Outlets Quit Pentagon Rather Than Sign Hegseth's Press Restrictions
